summary:
"After the Signal" is an educational website that helps learners ages 10–14 discover what six NASA missions left behind on the Moon and Mars. Visitors start on the website, where they can explore interactive mission maps, take short quizzes, and browse a mission archive with historical photographs and direct links to NASA sources. The "Interactive Game" section takes learners to an expedition which is a browser game where they pilot a rocket, climb rocky terrain, and answer questions to verify artifacts before returning their mission logs to Earth.

The project addresses the challenge by connecting hardware left on other worlds to the science it made possible. Learners discover how an Apollo retroreflector helps measure the Earth to Moon distance and how a Mars lander’s seismometer recorded marsquakes. The game gives learners a reason to apply what they read, while the archive gives curious students and teachers a place to explore the original evidence.
details:
After the Signal: is an interactive website and browser game that helps young learners discover what six NASA missions left behind on the Moon and Mars, and how that hardware helped scientists study both missions abandoned after mars or lunar missions.

How it works: Visitors can explore Moon and Mars mission maps, select landing sites, examine archival photographs, and answer short questions using evidence from the mission records. In the Artifact Expedition game, players pilot a rocket from Earth to the Moon and Mars, navigate rocky terrain, and climb to reach six artifacts. At each site, they read a mission briefing and answer a question to verify the artifact. An incorrect answer leaves the artifact unverified and offers a different question on the next attempt. To finish, players return to Earth and submit their verified mission logs at a simulated NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL).

Benefits and intended impact: We designed the project for learners ages 10–14, with families and classrooms also in mind. The maps let visitors explore at their own pace, while the game gives them a reason to recall and apply what they read. Our goal is for learners to explain what a piece of hardware did and what it helped scientists discover. For example, they can connect Apollo 11’s retroreflector to measurements of the Earth to Moon distance and the Mars lander’s seismometer to the study of Mars’s interior.

Tools and technology: We built the website and game with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The game uses HTML Canvas to render the astronaut, terrain, and hardware. We developed and edited the project in VS Code, organized the files in GitHub, and hosted the public submission on Hugging Face Static Spaces. We used NASA and JPL mission records and imagery to ground the educational content. The project runs in a web browser and requires no specialized hardware.

Creativity and design choices: We turned a mission archive into an expedition where players earn each verified log by reaching a site and understanding its science. We kept the historical mission records identifiable within the fictional game and linked to original sources so learners can explore further. Our team considered scientific accuracy, age appropriate explanations, keybind and touch controls, and how to balance exploration with clear guidance. We added landing markers and refined the astronaut’s camera view so players can focus on navigating and learning.
